title: Prescribed as for those before
hookLine: fasting prescribed so you may be mindful, and Allah wants ease for you (2:183–185)
last: BIRR — RIGHTEOUSNESS IS WHAT YOU DO.

lines: THREE VERSES THAT SET THE FAST.
cards: Imagine a rule that's strict on paper: no food, no water, from before dawn until sunset, for a whole month. Now read the fine print, and it's generous. Sick?
Don't fast; make it up later. Traveling? The same.
Too old or frail to fast at all? Feed someone in need instead. Most rules get harder in the fine print.
This one gets kinder, in the same three verses that set the fast. Today: sawm.

teach.h: SO THAT YOU MAY BE MINDFUL
teach.b: Last year you met the opening of this passage: fasting is prescribed for you, as it was for those before you, so that you may be mindful.
That last word is taqwa, which you met two weeks ago on the first page of al-Baqarah; the fast is a school for it. Verse one hundred eighty-four: a set number of days.
Whoever is sick or on a journey, an equal number of other days. And for those who can fast only with great hardship, a ransom: feeding a poor person.
Verse one hundred eighty-five names the month, Ramadan, the month the Qur'an was sent down, repeats the exemption, and gives the reason behind it all.
In Pickthall's words: “Allah desireth for you ease; He desireth not hardship for you.”

The word for fasting is sawm; at root it means to hold back, to abstain. The Qur'an uses the same word for Maryam's vow of silence: a sawm from speech. Bukhari keeps a scene from a journey in Ramadan.

Some companions were fasting, some weren't, and Anas reports that neither group found fault with the other. Scholars across the schools teach that a traveler may choose, and that the sick should not harm themselves.
The fast is demanding, and Muslims take it seriously. But the verse that commands it also guards the people keeping it. Mindfulness is the goal; hardship isn't.

how: Muslims fast from dawn to sunset through Ramadan; the sick and travelers may postpone days and make them up later, and those who cannot fast at all, such as the very old, feed a person in need for each day missed.

games.q: the fine print — tap the pairs.

the sick and travelers make up the days later.

games.q: you're traveling with the Prophet in Ramadan. some companions are fasting, some aren't. what happens between the two groups?
o: the fasting ones scold the others.
they argue until the Prophet decides.
neither group finds fault with the other.
games.why: neither found fault, Anas reports in Bukhari. the traveler's choice was respected both ways.

practice: Only if it's safe for you, picture skipping one snack; if you're unwell, pregnant, or need regular food, picture skipping five minutes of scrolling instead.
Notice where it usually lives in your day, picture not reaching for it, and hold the small hunger lightly, without strain.

wordCard.voice: Sawm. Fasting; at root, holding back. Prescribed so you may be mindful, with ease written into it for the sick, the traveler and the frail. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: fasting, from a root meaning to hold back; also called siyam.

carryVoice: Your line: Allah wants ease for you. The fast is a school for mindfulness. Until tomorrow.
